{{< generated ch17-hero >}}

## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Connect commands through standard input and output, keeping diagnostics separate from data.
- Find literal text, anchored patterns and FASTA headers with `grep`.
- Count records, inspect columns and check category frequencies before an analysis.
- Filter tab-separated tables with `awk`, retain their headers and validate numeric fields.
- Make a documented text transformation with `sed` while preserving the original file.
- Recognise when CSV, sequence or molecular formats need a dedicated parser.
:::

## Lab

{{< generated ch17-labs >}}

The lab produces a small data-quality report from sample metadata, a synthetic compound table and a run log. Finish with the [checkpoint](checkpoint.html), then review the [key points](key-points.html).

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
Complete [Linux fundamentals](../ch16-linux-fundamentals/index.html), or be comfortable with paths, quoting and working in a Bash terminal. Download the [practice workspace](../index.html) and keep its raw files unchanged. All terminal examples run from the workspace root, with inputs in `data/raw/` and derived files in `results/`.
:::

The records are deliberately small and synthetic, so you can predict every answer. The habits transfer to large files; the invented measurements do not support biological or chemical conclusions. These tools complement the [pandas lessons](../../part-1-foundations/ch01-scientific-python/03-pandas-dataframes.html): use the shell for quick inspection and orchestration, and a proper table or domain parser when the file format requires one.
